response:
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on transformer activations are tools for decomposing residual stream or MLP activations into interpretable features — the hope is that each learned dictionary element corresponds to a coherent, human-legible concept. The central question here is: when you retrain or fine-tune an SAE on a distribution of activations that has shifted (due to model fine-tuning, domain shift, or prompt distribution change), do the learned features maintain stable semantic identity, or do they drift such that a feature index that previously tracked "medical terminology" now partially tracks something else? The key concepts are: feature splitting and merging under retraining (a single feature may split into two or collapse with another), the geometry of the activation manifold under distribution shift, and attribution — meaning the downstream causal credit assigned to each feature for model behaviors. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is that even when a feature's reconstruction loss looks fine after retraining, its causal role in the circuit may have silently changed — a feature that was a faithful proxy for a concept in the original distribution may now be co-activated with different upstream and downstream features, making prior mechanistic interpretations stale without any obvious signal that anything broke. The expert also knows that sparse coding solutions are non-unique: retraining on shifted data can discover an entirely rotated basis that achieves equivalent reconstruction while scrambling feature-to-concept correspondence, and cross-run feature matching heuristics (cosine similarity of decoder weights) will miss this when features don't move geometrically but change their activation contexts.

The key test is activation context auditing: for each matched feature pair, collect the top-k activating examples (k ≈ 200–500) from both pre- and post-shift corpora and compare the semantic distributions of those examples, not just the decoder weights. Anthropic's scaling monosemanticity work on Claude features used exactly this kind of top-activating-example inspection to assign semantic labels — the point is that two features can share a decoder direction while activating on entirely different input contexts if the activation manifold has rotated. More rigorously, you'd run a causal intervention test: ablate or clamp the feature in both SAE versions and measure the downstream logit or behavioral change on a fixed probe dataset that was carefully chosen to isolate the target concept (e.g., a set of sentences where the concept is unambiguous and controlling). If the feature is semantically stable, the intervention effect sizes and affected output token distributions should be similar across both SAE versions on matched inputs; if they diverge significantly, the geometric alignment is coincidental. A quantitative threshold that has been used informally in SAE work is checking whether the Jaccard similarity of top-activating token sets falls below ~0.3–0.4, which would flag drift even when cosine similarity of decoders exceeds 0.9. The hardest case — which this test can still miss — is when the concept itself has shifted in the corpus (e.g., "bank" starts appearing more in financial than geographic contexts post-shift), making both the feature and its activating examples move coherently, so the intervention test looks stable while the real-world referent has changed.

If a circuit explanation is built on a pre-shift SAE and the underlying model weights are then fine-tuned (not just the SAE retrained), what is the minimal set of components you would need to revalidate to determine whether the circuit explanation remains causally valid?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-3164)
response:
The minimal revalidation set has three components: (1) the SAE's reconstruction fidelity on post-fine-tune activations, measured by L0/L2 reconstruction error and variance explained — if the fine-tuned model's activations have moved off the manifold the SAE was trained on, all downstream attribution is unreliable before you even check the circuit; (2) the causal efficacy of each node in the original circuit, verified by re-running activation patching or path patching on the original probe dataset using the fine-tuned model, checking whether each edge's patching effect (in logit difference units) has changed beyond a threshold (Wang et al.'s IOI circuit work used ~0.1–0.2 logit difference as a meaningful effect size floor); and (3) the input-output behavior of the circuit's proposed function on the probe dataset, meaning you check whether the fine-tuned model still performs the target behavior at all, since a circuit explanation is vacuously valid if the behavior has been ablated by fine-tuning. What you do not need to revalidate from scratch is the internal structure of nodes that patching confirms are still causally active — if an attention head's patching effect is preserved, you can provisionally trust its pre-shift QK/OV decomposition until edge-level evidence suggests otherwise. The non-obvious omission most people make is failing to check virtual weights — the effective weight matrices composed across layers that the circuit implicitly relies on — because fine-tuning even a single MLP layer can silently alter composed paths without changing any individual node's direct patching effect, producing a circuit that looks valid node-by-node but has broken information routing at the path level.

The key number to watch is the effective dimensionality of the residual stream subspace used by the circuit — measurable as the participation ratio of the covariance matrix restricted to circuit-relevant token positions — because routing corruption typically compresses or rotates this subspace in ways that precede any behavioral change detectable at the output.

When you use SAE feature activations to gate a corrective steering intervention, how do you prevent the gating mechanism itself from becoming a new point of mechanistic opacity that undermines the interpretability goal the circuit explanation was meant to serve?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-3167)
response:
The core discipline is to constrain the gating mechanism to be interpretability-first by construction: rather than learning an arbitrary classifier over SAE feature activations, you express the gate as a Boolean or soft conjunction over a small set of named features (e.g., "fire correction if feature 4821 'indirect object context' AND feature 7603 'proper noun in object position' are both active above threshold"), making the gating condition a human-readable logical formula that can itself be audited, patched, and falsified. This approach is directly supported by Marks et al.'s sparse feature circuits (2024), which demonstrated that behaviors in GPT-2 medium can be explained by circuits involving as few as 5–20 features with explicit logical dependencies — if your gate requires more features than this to be precise, that is a signal the intervention is underspecified, not a justification for opacity. The transparency requirement propagates recursively: each feature in the gate must itself have a validated semantic label (confirmed by top-activating example audits and causal intervention tests as discussed earlier), so the gate's interpretability is only as strong as the weakest feature label in the conjunction — you document this dependency explicitly as part of the intervention specification. A practical safeguard is to ablation-test the gate's components individually: if removing any single feature from the conjunction causes the gate to misfire on more than ~5% of probe examples, the gate is relying on a feature interaction you haven't explained, which is the opacity signal you need to resolve before deployment. The deeper principle is that the gating mechanism should be treated as a circuit node in its own right, subject to the same revalidation requirements as any other node — meaning it must appear in the circuit diagram, have documented input/output behavior, and be re-checked whenever the SAE is retrained or the model is fine-tuned, rather than being treated as external scaffolding that sits outside the interpretability accounting.

response:
A gate requiring 20+ features to achieve acceptable precision is strong evidence that the original circuit explanation was causally sufficient but not causally complete — it identified a pathway that works on the training distribution of the explanation, but the actual computation the model performs is conditioned on context that the explanation abstracted away, and that abstracted context is now surfacing as necessary gating conditions. This maps directly onto the distinction Geiger et al. draw in their interchange intervention work between a model that is consistent with a causal abstraction and one that implements it: the original circuit may have passed patching tests while the model was implicitly relying on auxiliary features that happened to be correlated with the probe distribution, and the 20+ feature gate is measuring the size of that implicit correlation structure. Concretely, Marks et al.'s sparse feature circuits found that even relatively simple behaviors in GPT-2 medium involved non-trivial feature fan-in at key nodes — if your gate is 4× larger than their full circuit explanations, you are not patching a circuit, you are discovering that the behavior has a much larger computational support than the original explanation acknowledged. The calibrated confidence adjustment is significant: you should treat the original explanation's causal claims as lower bounds on mechanistic complexity rather than complete accounts, which means any safety or alignment conclusion drawn from the explanation (e.g., "this model performs X via mechanism Y and therefore cannot do Z") needs to be re-examined, because the undocumented features in the gate could in principle support behaviors the explanation ruled out. The actionable response is not to abandon the explanation but to treat the gate's feature set as a research agenda: each feature beyond the original circuit's scope is a candidate for a missing node, and systematically checking whether those features have causal edges into the circuit's known nodes will either extend the explanation to completeness or reveal that the behavior is implemented by multiple overlapping circuits — a superposition of mechanisms that is fundamentally harder to interpret than a single clean pathway.
